choices: Any software that connects to the internet
Running software and storing data on someone else's servers, accessed on demand over the internet
A specific brand of server hardware
Software that only runs inside a web browser
questions.explanation: Cloud computing is defined by how you access and pay for computing capacity — on demand, from someone else's infrastructure — not by any specific technology or location.

questions.q: In the IaaS / PaaS / SaaS spectrum, what changes as you move from IaaS toward SaaS?
choices: Nothing — they're marketing terms for the same thing
You get more control but less convenience
The provider manages more of the stack, and you get more convenience in exchange for less control
Only the price changes; the underlying management is identical
questions.explanation: IaaS hands you raw infrastructure with the most control; SaaS hands you a finished product with the least control. Convenience and provider-managed scope both increase as you move up the stack.

questions.q: What is elasticity, in the context of cloud computing?
choices: A pricing discount for long-term contracts
The physical flexibility of server hardware
The ability to scale capacity up or down automatically based on real demand
A type of database used only by cloud providers
questions.explanation: Elasticity is what separates cloud computing from simply renting a fixed server — capacity adjusts automatically to match actual traffic, instead of being sized for a worst-case day.

questions.q: Why can cloud costs sometimes spike unexpectedly, in a way on-prem costs generally don't?
choices: Cloud providers change their prices daily without notice
Elastic, usage-based billing scales automatically with demand — including demand caused by bugs, spikes, or forgotten resources left running
On-prem hardware is always more expensive, so cloud costs just look higher by comparison
Cloud bills are fixed regardless of usage, so this isn't actually possible
questions.explanation: The same elasticity that makes cloud computing efficient also means costs scale automatically with usage — a bug, traffic spike, or forgotten test resource can drive up a bill with no human in the loop until the invoice arrives.
